title: Adaptive Recurrence Allocation: Learning When to Think Harder in Latent Reasoning Models
description: Problem: Current recurrent depth models apply a fixed or manually-chosen number of iterations uniformly across all input tokens and problem difficulties, wasting compute on easy inputs while potentially under-thinking hard ones. This inefficiency limits practical deployment of latent reasoning models. Proposed Method: We introduce an input-conditioned recurrence controller that dynamically allocates iteration depth per-token or per-sequence using a lightweight gating network trained with a compute-regularized objective. The controller predicts a halting probability at each recurrent step (inspired by Adaptive Computation Time) but operates entirely in latent space without token generation overhead. We augment the loss with a difficulty-calibrated compute penalty that encourages fewer iterations on easy examples (determined by confidence of output distribution) and more on hard ones. The controller is trained jointly with the recurrent block using a mixture of standard next-token prediction and reasoning benchmark supervision. Experiments: We train 1B and 3.5B parameter models on the same 800B token corpus as the anchor paper. We evaluate (1) reasoning benchmark accuracy vs. average iterations used, (2) compute-accuracy Pareto curves compared to fixed-iteration baselines, (3) correlation between allocated iterations and ground-truth problem difficulty across math, coding, and logic tasks, and (4) wall-clock inference speedup on easy vs. hard problem distributions.

title: Adaptive Halting in Latent Recurrent Reasoners: Learning When to Stop Thinking
description: Problem: Current recurrent depth models (like the anchor paper) require manually specifying the number of recurrent iterations at test-time, creating a dilemma: too few iterations underperform on hard problems, while too many waste compute on easy ones. There is no principled mechanism for the model to decide when its latent reasoning has converged. Proposed Method: We introduce a learned adaptive halting mechanism inspired by Graves' ACT (Adaptive Computation Time) but operating over latent recurrent iterations rather than token steps. A lightweight halting network observes the latent state after each iteration and predicts a stopping probability. During training, we add a regularization penalty on total iterations used (ponder cost) alongside task loss, encouraging the model to converge quickly when possible. We also explore an uncertainty-based halting criterion where iteration stops when the KL divergence between consecutive latent states falls below a learned threshold. Planned Experiments: (1) Train 1B and 3.5B parameter recurrent depth models with adaptive halting on standard language modeling corpora. (2) Evaluate compute-accuracy Pareto curves on GSM8K, MATH, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU, comparing fixed vs. adaptive iteration budgets. (3) Analyze per-problem iteration distributions to verify that harder problems receive more iterations. (4) Measure wall-clock inference speedup over fixed maximum-iteration baselines.

(2) We analyze recurrence depth distributions to verify alignment with token-level difficulty. (3) We measure FLOPs-vs-accuracy Pareto curves against chain-of-thought baselines. title: Adaptive Recurrence Allocation: Learning When and Where to Think Harder in Latent Reasoning Models
description: Problem: Current recurrent depth models apply uniform iteration counts across all tokens and input positions, wasting compute on trivial tokens while potentially under-allocating on critical reasoning steps. This rigid allocation limits efficiency and peak performance. Proposed Method: We introduce a learned adaptive gating mechanism that dynamically allocates recurrent iterations per token position based on input complexity signals. Specifically, we train a lightweight 'difficulty predictor' head that estimates required depth at each position using a differentiable halting mechanism inspired by Adaptive Computation Time (ACT), but operating over latent recurrence iterations rather than network layers. We incorporate a sparsity-inducing regularizer to encourage early halting on simple tokens while permitting deep iteration on complex reasoning pivots. Crucially, we train this gating end-to-end jointly with the recurrent block using a budget-constrained objective balancing accuracy and average compute expenditure. Experiments: (1) We evaluate on standard reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ARC, BBH) comparing uniform vs. adaptive allocation at matched FLOPs budgets; (2) We analyze which token positions receive high iteration counts to interpret model reasoning behavior; (3) We ablate gating architectures and regularization strengths; (4) We measure wall-clock speedups on hardware. We expect adaptive models to match or exceed uniform models at 40-60% of the compute cost.

title: AdaptiveDepth: Input-Conditioned Recurrence Allocation for Latent Reasoning Models
description:
Problem: Current recurrent depth models apply a fixed or manually-chosen number of latent iterations uniformly across all inputs at test time, wasting compute on simple queries while potentially under-allocating for hard ones. Determining the right depth per-instance is an open challenge that directly impacts the efficiency-performance tradeoff.

Proposed Method: We introduce a lightweight 'depth controller' — a small auxiliary network that observes the hidden state trajectory during recurrent iterations and predicts a stopping signal (analogous to adaptive computation time, but operating over latent reasoning steps). The controller learns to detect convergence in latent space by monitoring the L2 distance between successive hidden states and a learned 'uncertainty' embedding. We train it jointly with the recurrent backbone using a compute-regularized objective that penalizes unnecessary iterations while preserving accuracy. Additionally, we introduce a 'difficulty curriculum' during training, exposing the model to problems of varying complexity so the controller learns calibrated depth allocation.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark accuracy vs. average iterations on GSM8K, MATH, and ARC-Challenge compared to fixed-depth baselines. (2) FLOPs-matched comparison against chain-of-thought models. (3) Analysis of depth allocation distributions across problem difficulties. (4) Ablation on the stopping criterion design. (5) Scaling study from 1B to 7B parameters examining whether adaptive behavior emerges more reliably at larger scales.
